01 / THE DATA

Satellite-derived, not invented.

ESA WorldCover 2021 v200 is a land-cover classification based on Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 observations. We use a fixed Hyderabad study window (78.25–78.65° E, 17.22–17.60° N), not the official city boundary.

Python and Rasterio clip the original 10 m data and generalize it to a 100 m UTM grid using the most common source class per output cell. Small features can disappear. All displayed areas describe this generalized grid.

Explore the source ↗
02 / THE EXPERIMENT

Rules you can challenge.

We rank eligible land by distance to mapped development and the proportion of built-up cells in a surrounding 1.5 km window. Higher-priority cells fill first. Your expansion budget is spread linearly from 2021 to 2050.

Water, wetlands, snow, and no-data cells are excluded. You can also exclude mapped tree cover. These are model rules, not evidence that future development will respect those boundaries.

Download the Python starter ↗
03 / THE LIMITS

A scenario, not a forecast.

This is not a trained or validated urban-growth model. We have not measured 2000–2025 growth or validated future locations. There are no house counts, population forecasts, zoning rules, flood models, or climate projections.

The baseline classification itself can contain errors. Treat the results as an interactive thought experiment for discussing trade-offs, not planning advice. Historical back-testing and independent reference data would be needed for predictive claims.

Class mapping, provenance & reproducibility

Built-up: WorldCover 50. Vegetation & crops: 10, 20, 30, 40, 90, 95, 100. Water: 80. Other: 60, 70. No-data: 0 (excluded from statistics). The tree switch protects class 10; wetlands 90 and mangroves 95 are always protected. All classified grid cells have an area of 0.01 km².

Ranking score = distance to built-up (in 100 m cells) − 7 × neighborhood built-up fraction + small seeded tie-breaker. Existing built-up cells never disappear. If demand exceeds eligible land, allocation stops and the unfilled demand is shown. The Python download includes the actual extracted grid, its source URL, preparation code, and a local Streamlit explorer.
